text: Megalodon was the biggest shark that ever lived, and one of the largest [[predator|predators]] ever. Most scientists estimate it grew to about 15–20 m long. That is longer than a city bus, and roughly the length of a Mumbai local train coach. It may have weighed several times as much as a large elephant.

But nobody knows exactly. A shark's skeleton is made of [[cartilage|cartilage]], the bendy material in your ears and nose, which rarely becomes a [[@fossils-form|fossil]]. Almost everything we know about Megalodon comes from its teeth, plus a few [[fossil|fossil]] backbones. Scientists compare these with living sharks to estimate its size, and different methods give different answers.

st.reveal: Sharks have skeletons of cartilage, the bendy material in your nose and ears. It usually rots away before it can turn to stone. Teeth are much harder, and sharks shed thousands in a lifetime, so teeth are what survive.

d.try: Hold a ruler up to your hand. A big Megalodon tooth measured about 18 cm along its edge, roughly the length of a grown-up's hand. A great white shark's tooth is usually under 7 cm. Draw both side by side on paper to see the difference.
myth: Megalodon may still be alive in the deep ocean.

Megalodon became extinct about 3.6 million years ago. A huge warm-bodied shark would need lots of food near the surface and would leave fresh teeth everywhere. None have been found. A 2013 TV programme claiming it was still alive was fiction made to look real.

sec.h: Teeth as long as your hand
sec.t:
Megalodon's name means "big tooth", and its teeth are some of the most common large fossils in the world. The biggest are triangular, with jagged edges like a steak knife, and about 18 cm along the slanting edge.

Like other [[@sharks-old|sharks]], Megalodon grew new teeth all its life. They sat in rows, and when a front tooth broke or fell out, one from behind moved forward, a bit like a conveyor belt. A single shark might shed thousands of teeth. That is very different from people, who get just two sets of [[@teeth|teeth]] in a lifetime.

Megalodon teeth have been found on every continent except Antarctica, from the coasts of North Carolina and Florida to Japan, Australia and Europe. Fossil hunters often find them on beaches and in rivers.

{{story:teeth}}

Scientists estimate Megalodon's size by comparing its teeth with those of living sharks, especially the great white. Bigger sharks have bigger teeth, so the tooth size gives a rough body length.

A fossil from Belgium helped. It is a set of backbones from one Megalodon, and from it, researchers built a 3D model of a shark about 16 m long. Some recent studies suggest Megalodon may have had a longer, slimmer body than a great white, which would change the estimates. That is why most books give a range rather than a single number.

Megalodon lived from about 23 to 3.6 million years ago in warm seas around the world. It hunted big prey: dolphins, seals, sea turtles and whales. Fossil whale bones have been found with deep bite marks that match Megalodon's teeth.

Young Megalodons probably grew up in shallow, warm coastal waters, where there were fewer big predators. Fossil sites in Panama and elsewhere hold many small Megalodon teeth together, which suggests these were nursery areas, much like the ones some sharks use today.

In 2023, scientists studied chemicals in Megalodon teeth and suggested it was warmer than the water around it, by around 7 °C. Being warm-bodied may have helped it swim fast and hunt in cooler water, but it also meant it needed huge amounts of food.

Megalodon became [[extinct|extinct]] about 3.6 million years ago. Scientists think several things combined. The oceans cooled, and some of its favourite prey, smaller whales, declined. Great white sharks, which were spreading through the oceans at around that time, may have competed with it for food.

A modern [[@blue-whale|blue whale]] is longer and far heavier than even the biggest estimates for Megalodon. Sharks themselves are still here, with over 500 living [[species|species]], and you can see Megalodon's teeth in many [[@dino-museums|natural history museums]] today.

text: In 2013, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) launched the Mars Orbiter Mission, nicknamed Mangalyaan, which means "Mars craft".

Its rocket, the [[@isro-launch|PSLV]], was not powerful enough to throw it straight to Mars. So engineers fired Mangalyaan's own engine near Earth again and again, stretching its [[orbit|orbit]] a little more each time. Then one big push sent it on its way. On 24 September 2014, after 298 days in space, it reached Mars orbit. No country had ever done that on its first try.

d.try: Put a small plate in the middle of a big sheet of paper for the Sun. Draw Earth's path around it, and Mars's bigger path outside that. Mars takes about 687 days to go round once. Mangalyaan's trip took 298 days, so mark where Mars was at launch and where it had moved to on arrival. You have to aim at where Mars will be, not where it is.
myth: Mangalyaan landed on Mars.
Mangalyaan was an orbiter. It circled Mars and studied it from above, from as close as about 420 km to as far as tens of thousands of kilometres. It never touched the ground.

sec.t:
Think of a child on a jhoola. Each push at the right moment sends the [[@how-swings|swing a little higher]]. Mangalyaan worked the same way. For almost a month, every time it came closest to Earth, its engine fired and its loop around Earth grew longer.

On 1 December 2013, the final burn sent it out of Earth's grip. After that, it coasted around the Sun for months with its engine off. ISRO had aimed it at the spot where Mars would be in ten months' time, not where Mars was on launch day.

The whole mission cost about ₹450 crore, roughly 74 million US dollars. That was less than the budget of the Hollywood space film *Gravity*. ISRO saved money by using a proven rocket, a small spacecraft, and lots of careful planning instead of extra power.

NASA's MAVEN spacecraft reached Mars just two days earlier, on 21 September 2014. The two agencies' teams sent each other congratulations. A photo of women scientists at ISRO celebrating in saris was shared around the world, and helped many girls picture themselves working in space science. Mangalyaan's picture later appeared on the back of India's ₹2,000 note.

Mangalyaan carried five small science instruments. Its colour camera photographed whole sides of Mars at once, including giant dust storms and the planet's two tiny moons, Phobos and Deimos. Other instruments studied the thin air and searched for methane gas.

Mangalyaan's orbit was long and stretched, so at its farthest it was tens of thousands of kilometres from Mars. From there, its camera could fit the whole planet into a single frame, volcanoes, clouds and all, something orbiters flying low cannot do.

It was designed to last six months. Instead, it kept working for about eight years. In 2022, ISRO lost contact with it, probably after its batteries ran down during a long [[eclipse|eclipse]], when Mars blocked the sunlight its [[@solar-panels|solar panels]] needed.

Mangalyaan showed that a young space agency could reach another planet on a tight budget. Since then, ISRO has landed on the Moon with [[@chandrayaan|Chandrayaan-3]] and sent [[@aditya-l1|Aditya-L1]] to study the [[@sun-what|Sun]]. If you want to see what Mars is like from the ground, read about [[@mars-rovers|the rovers driving there]].

text: The stars are so far away that kilometres become useless for measuring them. So [[astronomer|astronomers]] use the [[lightyear|light-year]]: the distance light travels in one year.

Light is the fastest thing there is. It covers about 3,00,000 km every second, enough to go around Earth more than seven times. In a year, it travels about 9.5 trillion km. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away. That is roughly 40 trillion km. A car driving nonstop at 100 km/h [[@maths-speed-time|would need about 45 million years]] to get there.

d.try: Hold one thumb up at arm's length. Close your left eye and line your thumb up with something across the room. Now switch eyes. Your thumb seems to jump. Astronomers use the same trick, called parallax, with Earth's two sides of its orbit as their two "eyes", to measure how far away the nearer stars are.
myth: A light-year is a measure of time.
Despite the word "year", a light-year is a distance. It is how far light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres.

sec.t:
Because light takes time to travel, you never see anything exactly as it is now. Moonlight is just over a second old when it reaches you. Sunlight is [[@what-if-sun-vanished|about 8 minutes and 20 seconds old]].

Starlight is far older. The bright star Sirius is about 8.6 light-years away, so its light left before many readers of this article were born. Some of the stars you can see on a dark night are hundreds or even thousands of light-years away. When you look at the most distant of them, you are looking at light that set out before the [[@taj-mahal|Taj Mahal]] was built.

People once argued about whether light took any time at all to travel. In 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer noticed that Jupiter's moon Io slipped behind Jupiter a few minutes late whenever Earth was farther from Jupiter. The light was taking longer to reach us. From this he made one of the first estimates of its speed.

Measuring the distance to a star was even harder. The trick that finally worked is called parallax. Hold up a finger and look at it with one eye, then the other. It seems to jump against the background.

Earth makes the same jump on a giant scale as it goes around the Sun. Astronomers photograph a star in January and again in July, from opposite sides of Earth's [[orbit|orbit]]. Nearby stars seem to shift very slightly against faraway ones. Measuring that tiny shift gives the distance. In 1838, the German astronomer Friedrich Bessel became the first to do it, for a star called 61 Cygni, about 11 light-years away.

{{story:big-numbers}}

Today, the European Space Agency's Gaia spacecraft has measured the positions of more than a billion stars, again and again, from 1.5 million km away. From those tiny shifts, scientists have built the most detailed 3D map of our [[galaxy|galaxy]] ever made.

For stars too far away for parallax, astronomers use other clues, such as how bright a certain kind of star really is compared with how bright it looks. Each method checks the next, like rungs on a ladder.

Our galaxy, the [[@milky-way|Milky Way]], is about 1,00,000 light-years across. The Andromeda Galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away, is the farthest thing most people can see without a telescope, from a really dark place.

The [[@webb-telescope|Webb telescope]] catches light from [[@galaxies|galaxies]] that left them more than 13 billion years ago, when the universe was young. Even our fastest spacecraft are slow by comparison. Voyager 1 would need more than 70,000 years to travel as far as Proxima Centauri. To learn how the stars themselves form and shine, read [[@stars-born|how stars are born]], or see how sunlight is scattered on its last few kilometres to make [[@sky-blue|our sky blue]].

text: Mercury is the smallest of the eight [[@planets-size|planets]] and the closest to the Sun. It is a grey, rocky ball covered in [[crater|craters]], a little bigger than our Moon. It has almost no air at all.

Without air to hold in heat, Mercury swings between extremes. In sunlight, the ground reaches about 430 °C, hot enough to melt lead. At night it drops to about −180 °C. Standing on Mercury, the Sun would look about three times wider than it does from Earth, in a black sky.

d.try: Work out your age on Mercury. Multiply your age in years by 365 to get your age in days, then divide by 88. A 10-year-old on Earth is about 41 Mercury years old. Now try your parents' ages.
myth: Mercury always keeps the same side facing the Sun.

Astronomers believed this for decades. In 1965, radar signals bounced off Mercury from the Arecibo telescope in Puerto Rico showed that it does spin, once every 59 Earth days. Every part of Mercury gets its turn in the sunlight.
facts: about 430 °C by day, about −180 °C at night

sec.h: A year shorter than a day
sec.t:
Mercury races around the [[@sun-what|Sun]] faster than any other planet. One lap takes just 88 Earth days. That's its year.

But it [[@space-weird-day-longer-year|spins very slowly]], turning once every 59 Earth days. Put those two motions together, and the time from one sunrise to the next is about 176 Earth days. So a single Mercury day lasts two Mercury years. If you lived there, your birthday would come round twice between breakfast and the following breakfast.

Mercury's [[orbit|orbit]] is also stretched into an oval. From some spots on the surface, the Sun would appear to rise, stop, go backwards a little, then carry on across the sky.

Mercury has a huge iron core, filling most of its inside. As that core slowly cooled over billions of years, the planet shrank, like an apple drying out and wrinkling. Its rocky crust cracked and buckled into long cliffs, some of them hundreds of kilometres long and over a kilometre high.

Scientists think Mercury's radius has shrunk by several kilometres. Its giant core also gives it a weak magnetic field, something [[@venus-hot|Venus]] and Mars lack.

Getting to Mercury is surprisingly hard. A spacecraft falling towards the Sun speeds up, so it has to brake a lot to slip into orbit. Only a few missions have tried.

NASA's Mariner 10 flew past three times in 1974 and 1975. MESSENGER mapped the whole planet, then ran out of fuel and crashed into it in 2015. BepiColombo, a joint mission by Europe and Japan launched in 2018, has been looping past Earth, Venus and Mercury itself to slow down. It was built to put two spacecraft into orbit around Mercury.

Mercury never strays far from the Sun in our sky, so you can only see it low on the horizon just after sunset or just before sunrise. In [[@hindi-language|Hindi]], Mercury is Budh, which gives Wednesday its name, Budhvaar. Many old [[@calendars|calendars]] around the world named the days of the week after the Sun, the Moon and the five planets people could see. In French, Wednesday is mercredi, named after the same planet. Every few years, Mercury crosses in front of the Sun as a tiny black dot. The next time will be in 2032.

text: Meteorites are rocks from space that survive the fall through Earth's air and land on the ground. Most are made of stone, similar to rocks on Earth but often containing tiny round grains. Some are made almost entirely of [[@asteroid-mining|iron and nickel metal]]. A few are a mix of the two, with green crystals set in shiny metal.

Nearly all meteorites are broken pieces of [[asteroid|asteroids]], most from the belt between Mars and Jupiter. A small number came from Mars or the Moon, knocked off by big impacts. Many are older than any rock on Earth, so they tell scientists what the [[solar-system|solar system]] was made of when it was brand new.

st.prompt: Where in the world are the most meteorites found?
st.reveal: Dark rocks lying on white ice are easy to spot. Moving ice also carries meteorites along and piles them up in certain places. Expeditions have collected tens of thousands of meteorites in Antarctica since the 1970s.

d.try: Collect a few stones from a garden or beach. For each, ask the questions meteorite hunters ask. Does it feel heavier than it looks? Does a fridge magnet stick to it? Does it have a thin, dark, smooth crust? Most stones will fail every test. Even experts say most rocks people bring in turn out to be "meteorwrongs".
myth: Meteorites are red-hot or on fire when they hit the ground.
The outer layer melts as the rock rushes through the air, but that only lasts a few seconds. Then it slows down and falls like a stone. Most meteorites land cool or just warm to the touch.
facts: stony, more than 9 in every 10 falls

sec.t:
These three words are easy to mix up. While a space rock is still in space, it is a meteoroid. When it hits Earth's air and glows as a streak of light, that streak is a [[meteor|meteor]], or [[@shooting-stars|shooting star]]. If any of it reaches the ground, that piece is a meteorite.

Most meteoroids are no bigger than a grain of sand and burn up completely. Only rocks at least the size of a pebble or a fist, moving fairly slowly, survive to land.

More than nine out of ten meteorites seen falling are stony. Most of these are chondrites, packed with chondrules, little round beads of rock that melted and cooled in space before the planets formed. Some chondrites also contain specks of white mineral that are the oldest solid material known, about 4.57 billion years old. Like Earth's [[@rocks-types|rocks]], they are made of minerals, but they have barely changed since they formed.

{{story:rocks-types}}

Iron meteorites are chunks of the metal cores of small worlds that melted, separated into layers and later broke apart. When an iron meteorite is cut, polished and treated, it shows a striking criss-cross pattern of metal crystals that can only grow while metal cools extremely slowly, over millions of years. They are heavy, and a [[@magnets-how|magnet]] sticks to them strongly.

Stony-iron meteorites are the rarest. Some, called pallasites, are among the most beautiful rocks known, with golden-green olivine crystals in metal.

The largest meteorite ever found is the Hoba meteorite in Namibia, a slab of iron weighing about 60 tonnes. It was found by a farmer in 1920 and is too heavy to move, so it still lies where it landed.

The Willamette meteorite, about 15.5 tonnes, is the largest found in the United States and is on display at the American Museum of Natural History in New York. The Grand Ronde people of Oregon hold it sacred, and they and the museum reached an agreement in 2000 that allows them to visit it for ceremonies.

In 1954, in Sylacauga, Alabama, a meteorite crashed through a house roof, bounced off a radio and hit a woman named Ann Hodges as she napped on her sofa. She was left with a large bruise. It is the best-documented case of a person being hit.

India has its own falls. In June 2017, a rare carbon-rich meteorite fell at Mukundpura, near [[@jaipur|Jaipur]], and scientists studied it for clues to the chemistry of the early solar system.

[[@antarctica|Antarctica]] is the best place on Earth to find meteorites. Dark rocks stand out on white ice, and slowly moving [[@glaciers|glaciers]] carry them to certain areas where wind strips the ice away, leaving them on the surface. Teams have recovered tens of thousands of meteorites there.

Some contain amino [[acid|acids]], the building blocks of [[protein|proteins]], made in space. The Murchison meteorite, which fell in Australia in 1969, contains tiny grains of stardust older than the Sun. Holding a meteorite is the closest most of us will come to touching another world.

text: The solar wind is a stream of electrically charged particles that flows out from the Sun in every direction, all the time. It is mostly [[proton|protons]] and [[electron|electrons]], the tiny pieces that atoms are made of. It comes from the Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona, which is so hot, over a million degrees, that the Sun's gravity can't hold on to all of it.
The wind usually travels at about 400 km per second, and fast streams can reach 800 km per second or more. At those speeds, it reaches Earth in about two to four days.

It is extremely thin. Near Earth, there are only a few particles in each cubic centimetre. Yet it shapes the tails of [[comet|comets]], lights up the auroras and fills a giant bubble around the whole [[solar-system|solar system]].

st.reveal: A comet's gas tail is blown by the solar wind, so it always points away from the Sun, whichever way the comet is moving. This clue helped scientists in the 1950s work out that the Sun must be blowing a steady wind.

d.try: Hang a few strips of tissue paper from a pencil and hold it in front of a fan on low, then walk slowly around the fan in a circle. Notice that the strips always point away from the fan, whichever way you are walking, just like a comet's tail in the solar wind.
myth: Space between the planets is completely empty.

It is far emptier than any vacuum made on Earth, but it is filled with the thin, fast solar wind, along with dust and magnetic fields. There are usually a few particles in every cubic centimetre near Earth.
facts: charged particles, mostly protons and electrons
about 400 km per second, sometimes 800 or more

sec.t:
In the 1950s, a German [[astronomer|astronomer]] named Ludwig Biermann noticed something odd about [[@comets|comets]]. Their gas tails always pointed away from the Sun, and sometimes rippled as if blown. He suggested the Sun was pushing out a steady stream of particles.

In 1958, an American physicist, Eugene Parker, worked out the maths and called it the "solar wind". Many scientists didn't believe him, and his paper was nearly rejected. In 1962, NASA's Mariner 2 spacecraft, on its way to Venus, measured the wind directly. Parker was right.

In 2018, NASA launched the Parker Solar Probe, which flies closer to the Sun than any spacecraft before it. It was the first NASA spacecraft named after a living person. Parker, then 91, watched the launch. He died in 2022.

Earth has a [[@earth-magnet|magnetic field]], made by molten iron swirling deep inside the planet. It acts like a shield, steering most of the solar wind around us.

Some particles leak in near the North and South Poles. They crash into gases high in the air and make them glow, creating the [[@aurora|aurora]], the northern and southern lights.

Mars has no global magnetic field. NASA's MAVEN spacecraft has found that the solar wind strips gas from the top of the Martian [[atmosphere|atmosphere]]. Over billions of years, this helped turn Mars from a world with rivers into a cold, dry desert.

{{story:earth-magnet}}

Sometimes the Sun throws out a huge cloud of particles called a coronal mass ejection. When one hits Earth, it can cause a geomagnetic storm. In March 1989, a storm like this caused a blackout across the Canadian province of Quebec, leaving millions of people without power for about nine hours.

Storms like these can damage [[@satellites-help|satellites]], confuse GPS and disturb radio signals. Astronauts on the space station have to be careful too. NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center in the USA issues warnings, a bit like a weather forecast for space. India's [[@aditya-l1|Aditya-L1]] [[observatory|observatory]], sitting about 1.5 million km from Earth towards the Sun, carries instruments that measure the solar wind before it reaches us.

The solar wind blows outwards until it runs into the thin gas between the stars. The bubble it carves out is called the heliosphere, and it surrounds all the planets.

In 2012, [[@voyager|Voyager 1]] became the first spacecraft to cross its edge, about 18 billion km from the Sun. Voyager 2 followed in 2018. Both are now sending back measurements from interstellar space, beyond the reach of the wind that has blown past every planet.

text: India's first satellite was called Aryabhata. It went into [[orbit|orbit]] on 19 April 1975, carried by a Soviet rocket from Kapustin Yar, a launch site in what is now Russia. It was built by Indian scientists and engineers at a small new facility in Peenya, on the edge of Bengaluru.

It weighed 360 kg, about as much as four grown men, and had 26 sides, most of them covered in solar cells. Its job was to study X-rays from space, the Sun and the upper [[atmosphere|atmosphere]]. Its three experiments came from Indian research labs, so every reading it sent down was new science done by Indians.
It was named after [[@aryabhata|Aryabhata]], the great Indian mathematician and [[astronomer|astronomer]] who lived about 1,500 years ago.

To make it look like a football
Because each side held a different camera

st.reveal: The satellite was not steered to point at the Sun all the time. With 26 faces, most of them covered in solar cells, there were always some panels catching sunlight as it spun.

d.try: Make a simple many-sided shape. Cut out several equal paper squares and triangles and tape them into a closed ball shape. Shine a torch at it from different sides and count how many faces catch the light each time. That was Aryabhata's trick for staying powered.
myth: India launched its first satellite on its own rocket.
Aryabhata was built in India but launched on a Soviet rocket. India's first satellite launched on an Indian rocket was Rohini, which flew on the SLV-3 in 1980.

sec.t:
In the early 1970s, India's space programme was tiny. Scientists had assembled small rockets in a church in Kerala, but nobody in India had ever built a satellite. Then, in 1972, the Soviet Union agreed to launch one, in return for letting Soviet ships use Indian ports.

A team led by the physicist U. R. Rao had about three years to build it. They worked in tin-roofed industrial sheds in Peenya. Many parts had to be designed from scratch, because they could not be bought. The budget was set at about 3 crore rupees.

The satellite's data reception centre in Bengaluru was squeezed into whatever space could be found. One part of it was a converted toilet.

{{story:aryabhata}}

Aryabhata was a [[polyhedron|polyhedron]], a solid shape with many flat faces, about 1.4 metres across. Picture something a bit taller than a school desk and a little rounder.

The satellite spun gently but did not point itself at the Sun. So the designers covered 24 of its 26 faces with solar cells. Whichever way it turned, some panels caught the light. That's the same idea behind a [[@shapes-3d|3D shape]] such as a football, which looks much the same from every angle.

After launch, signals poured in. But on about the fifth day in orbit, a fault in the power system cut off its science instruments. The experiments stopped. Aryabhata kept sending some signals for a while longer, which still let engineers learn how their satellite behaved in space.

On launch day, the news went out on All India Radio, and newspapers splashed it across their front pages. India had become one of only about a dozen countries with a satellite of its own. It stayed in orbit for almost 17 years, circling Earth silently, before falling back and burning up in the atmosphere in February 1992.

So was it a failure? Not really. Building and running Aryabhata taught India's engineers how to design satellites, track them and talk to them. Within a few years, India was building satellites for TV, weather and phones. The same team went on to build Bhaskara, an Earth-watching satellite, in 1979. [[@isro-missions|ISRO]] still runs its satellite centre in Bengaluru, now named after U. R. Rao.

In 1976, the Reserve Bank of India printed a picture of Aryabhata on the back of the two-rupee note. It stayed there until 1997. For two decades, millions of Indians carried India's first satellite in their pockets, often without knowing what the strange shape was.

Five years after Aryabhata, India launched a satellite on its own rocket for the first time, from Sriharikota in 1980. Today ISRO has sent missions to the Moon, Mars and the Sun. And it all began even more humbly than a toilet control room. Parts of India's very first rocket were carried to the launch pad [[@space-rocket-bicycle|on a bicycle]].

text: Most snakes lay eggs and leave. The king cobra mother builds a nest and guards it.
Rotting leaves in the nest give off warmth, like a [[compost|compost]] heap, keeping the eggs cosy.
King cobras are shy and avoid people. Never go near one. Always tell an adult.

The nest is built in the wet forests of India and South-East Asia, often before [[@monsoon|the monsoon]]. Inside a mound of leaves, the eggs stay warm and damp but protected from flooding, while the mother keeps egg-eating animals away.

Its scientific name, Ophiophagus, means ‘snake eater’. It mostly eats other snakes.

d.try: Build a model leaf nest. Gather a big pile of dry leaves in a corner of a garden or a large box. Push them together into a mound using only your forearms, with no hands, the way a king cobra uses its coils. Put a thermometer in the middle for a day and compare it with the air outside to see if the pile stays warmer.
myth: King cobras chase people and attack without warning.

King cobras are shy and usually slip away from people. When cornered, they rise up, spread their hood and give a low growl as a warning. Bites are rare. Most snakebite deaths in India come from four other snakes, not the king cobra.

sec.t:
A king cobra has no arms or claws, so she builds with her body. She loops her coils around fallen leaves and drags them into a pile, sometimes on a slope or at the foot of a [[@bamboo|bamboo]] clump. The finished nest can be over a metre across, with a chamber for eggs inside and a layer on top where she often rests.

She lays about 20 to 40 white, leathery eggs. Then she guards the nest for weeks, chasing off [[@lizards|monitor lizards]], mongooses and wild pigs. She usually leaves shortly before the eggs hatch, about two to three months after they were laid. The babies are already about 50 cm long and carry [[venom|venom]] from the moment they hatch, so they can look after themselves.

For a long time, scientists thought every king cobra belonged to one species, *Ophiophagus hannah*. But snakes from different regions looked slightly different, and their DNA told the same story. In 2024, a team of researchers split them into four species.

The king cobra of the Western Ghats got its own name, *Ophiophagus kaalinga*. Research at the Agumbe Rainforest Research Station in Karnataka, founded by the herpetologist Romulus Whitaker, helped show this. There, scientists have tracked king cobras with small radio tags to learn how far they travel, where they nest and how they live alongside farms and villages.

India has more snakebite deaths than any other country, tens of thousands every year. Almost all of them are caused by four snakes: the spectacled cobra, the common krait, the Russell's viper and the saw-scaled viper. King cobras live mostly in forests, avoid people, and bite rarely.

In many villages in Karnataka and Kerala, snakes are respected and even worshipped, and people call trained rescuers to move a king cobra rather than kill it. If you ever see a snake, stay still, back away slowly and tell an adult. Snakes don't chase people.

Caring for eggs is unusual among snakes but not among [[reptile|reptiles]]. Mother [[@croc-ancient|crocodiles]] guard their nests and carry their babies to the water. Some dinosaurs probably [[@dino-eggs|buried their eggs]] in warm mounds of soil and plants, much like the king cobra's leaf pile, and birds, the dinosaurs' living [[descendant|descendants]], are famous nest builders.

text: Everything is made of tiny [[atom|atoms]]. Each atom has even tinier particles called [[electron|electrons]], which carry a negative electric charge. Usually, things have a balanced amount of charge, so nothing happens.

When you rub [[@made-balloons|a balloon]] on your [[@hair-grow|hair]], some electrons get scraped off your hair and stick to the balloon. Now the balloon has extra electrons and a negative charge. Your hair has lost some and has a positive charge. Opposite charges attract, so the balloon and your hair pull towards each other and the balloon can cling.

This kind of electricity is called static, meaning it stays put instead of flowing through a wire like the [[@electricity-made|electricity]] in your home. It sits on the surface until it finds a way to escape, sometimes with a little spark.

st.prompt: After you rub a balloon on your hair, your hair strands fly apart from each other. Why?

options.t: Each strand has the same charge, and same charges push apart
The balloon has made the hair lighter

st.reveal: Rubbing moves electrons from your hair to the balloon. That leaves every strand with the same positive charge. Like charges repel, so the strands push away from each other and stand up, while being pulled towards the negatively charged balloon.

d.try: Blow up a balloon and rub it on dry hair or a woollen jumper for about ten seconds. Hold it near some tiny bits of torn tissue paper and watch them jump up. Then turn on a tap so a very thin stream of water flows, and bring the balloon close without touching. The stream will bend towards it.
myth: Static shocks happen because it's cold.

It's dry air, not cold, that makes static build up. Moist air lets extra charge slowly leak away. Winter air indoors is often very dry, which is why shocks are more common then, but a dry summer day can do the same.
facts: a giant spark of static electricity

sec.t:
Each strand of hair has lost electrons, so each one now carries a positive charge. Same charges push each other away. So your hairs try to get as far from one another as they can, and they spread out and stand up.

The same thing happens when you pull off a woollen sweater on a winter morning and hear tiny crackles. Those crackles are little sparks as charges jump between the sweater and your clothes or hair. In a dark room, you can sometimes see them flash.

Inside a thundercloud, ice crystals and soft hail bump into each other as air currents toss them up and down. Those collisions move charge around, much like rubbing a balloon. The top of the cloud becomes positive and the bottom negative. When the difference grows too big, the charge escapes as a gigantic spark: [[@lightning|lightning]].

In 1752, the American inventor [[@benjamin-franklin|Benjamin Franklin]] described flying a kite in a storm to show that [[@lightning-rods|lightning is electrical]]. It was a very dangerous experiment. In 1753, a scientist in Russia named Georg Richmann was killed by lightning while trying something similar. Franklin went on to invent the lightning rod, a metal rod that carries a strike safely into the ground.

Static isn't only a nuisance. [[@photocopiers|Photocopiers]] and [[@printers|laser printers]] use it to make powdered ink cling to exactly the right parts of the paper. Factory chimneys can use charged plates to pull smoke particles out of the air before they escape. Some car paint sprayers charge the paint so it wraps evenly around the metal.

Static can also be a danger. At petrol pumps, a spark near fuel vapour could start a fire, which is why pumps are carefully earthed and phone use is often discouraged. Workers who build [[@chips-silicon|computer chips]] wear special straps to stop static from frying the tiny [[circuit|circuits]].

text: Andy Warhol was an American artist who became the best-known face of pop art in the 1960s. Pop art took images from popular culture, such as adverts, comic strips, packaging and film stars, and put them into galleries. Warhol painted soup cans, bottles of Coca-Cola, dollar bills and rows of famous faces.

He liked his art to look as if a machine had made it. Using silkscreen printing, he made many copies of the same picture in different colours, like products rolling off a factory line. He even called his studio "the Factory". Some people thought this wasn't real art. Others thought it showed something true about a world full of brands, screens and celebrities.

st.prompt: How did Warhol make many copies of the same picture, such as a famous face, in different colours?

options.t: Silkscreen printing, pushing ink through a fine mesh stencil

st.reveal: In silkscreen printing, an image is transferred onto a stretched mesh. Ink is pressed through the open parts onto canvas or paper. By changing colours and repeating the print, Warhol could make rows of the same image, each slightly different.

myth: Andy Warhol definitely said "In the future, everyone will be famous for 15 minutes."

sec.t:
Warhol was born Andrew Warhola in 1928 in Pittsburgh, a steel-making city. His parents had moved to the USA from a village in what is now Slovakia. When he was about eight, he fell ill with a disease that affected his nerves and spent a long time in bed. His mother gave him [[@comics-art|comics]], colouring books and magazines with photos of film stars, and he drew constantly.

He studied design at college in Pittsburgh, then moved to [[@new-york|New York]] in 1949. There he became a successful commercial artist, drawing shoes, handbags and other products for magazine adverts.

Warhol wanted to be taken seriously as a painter. In 1962, a gallery in Los Angeles showed his *Campbell's Soup Cans*: 32 canvases, each showing a different flavour of the same cheap canned soup. They were lined up like goods on a shop shelf.

Visitors were puzzled. Why paint something so ordinary? Warhol said he had eaten Campbell's soup for lunch for years. To him, the cans were simply part of everyday American life. The paintings now belong to the Museum of Modern Art in New York and are among the most recognised artworks of the twentieth century.

Warhol was obsessed with fame. He made bright, repeated portraits of film stars and singers from news photographs. In 2022, one of his portraits of the actress Marilyn Monroe sold at auction for 195 million dollars. At the time, no work by an American artist had ever fetched more at auction.

He also enjoyed the idea that some things are the same for everyone. In a book published in 1975, he wrote that a president, a film star and a person on the street all drink the same Coke. No amount of money, he said, buys a better one. That is one reason he painted [[@soft-drinks|soft drinks]] and soup.

Many critics at the time felt that copying adverts and photos wasn't real art, and that Warhol was more interested in money and fame than ideas. Others argued that he held up a mirror to modern life, where people see the same images again and again on screens, shelves and billboards. The debate has never fully ended.

Warhol died in New York in 1987, aged 58, after a routine operation. The Andy Warhol Museum opened in Pittsburgh in 1994 and is one of the largest museums in the world devoted to a single artist.

Pop art spread far beyond America. In India, the painter [[@bhupen-khakhar|Bhupen Khakhar]] used the bright colours of calendar art and shop signs to paint ordinary people at work. Today, when a brand logo turns up on a T-shirt as a joke, or a meme repeats one face in many colours, it owes something to the man who painted soup.

text: Tattoos are at least about 5,300 years old. We know because of Ötzi, a man who died high in the Alps between Italy and Austria and was frozen in ice until hikers found him in 1991. His skin carries 61 tattoos: groups of short lines and small crosses, made with charcoal or soot. Experts once thought it was rubbed into tiny cuts, but a 2024 study suggests it was more likely poked in with a sharp point.

Since then, tattoos have turned up on ancient bodies from Egypt, Siberia and South America. People have tattooed for beauty, for healing, to show bravery or adulthood, to mark which group they belonged to, and to remember someone they loved.

st.prompt: Why does a tattoo last for years when a pen drawing on your skin washes off in a day?

options.t: The ink is put into a deeper skin layer that doesn't shed
Tattoo ink is a kind of glue
Tattoo ink soaks into the bone

st.reveal: The top layer of skin flakes away every few weeks, taking pen ink with it. Tattoo needles place ink in the dermis, the layer underneath, where it is trapped inside cells and stays put for decades.

n.certNote: Ötzi has the oldest tattoos most experts accept. Older claims, such as marks on some South American mummies, are still debated, and nobody knows exactly when people first tattooed.

myth: Tattoos are a modern fashion that started with sailors.
Sailors helped spread tattoos in Europe and America in the 1700s and 1800s, but people in Asia, Africa, the Americas and the Pacific had been tattooing for thousands of years before that.

sec.t:
Ötzi's tattoos aren't pictures. They're simple lines on his lower back, knees, ankles and wrists. Here's the strange part: many of them sit over joints where scans show he had wear and pain. Some researchers think the marks were part of a treatment, a little like acupuncture. Others say we can't be sure.

Ötzi was about 45, carried a copper axe and had eaten a meal of meat and grain shortly before he died. Scientists have studied him so closely that we know more about his body than about many people alive today.

The word "tattoo" came to English from Tahiti. Sailors on Captain James Cook's ship in 1769 wrote down the Tahitian word "tatau". Many sailors returned home with tattoos of their own.

Across the Pacific, [[@polynesians|Polynesian]] tattooing is ancient and sacred. In Samoa, the pe'a covers a man from the waist to the knees and can take weeks to finish, using combs of bone tapped with a stick. Māori tā moko in New Zealand carves lines into the skin of the face, showing a person's family and history.

India has long tattoo traditions, especially among [[@people-tribes-india|tribal communities]]. In central and eastern India, women of communities like the Baiga and Gond wear godna, patterns of dots and lines. Many believed godna were the only ornaments that stayed with you after death.

In Arunachal Pradesh, older Apatani women have facial tattoos, a custom that stopped in the 1970s. Among the Konyak Nagas, face tattoos once showed a warrior's deeds. Today these traditions are fading, but young artists are reviving the old patterns. A gentler cousin, [[@mehendi|mehendi]], stains only the top layer and fades in a couple of weeks.

In 1891, a New York tattoo artist named Samuel O'Reilly patented an electric tattoo machine, adapted from an electric pen designed by Thomas Edison. It made tattooing much faster.

A tattoo needle puts ink into the dermis, the layer under the outer skin. Your body treats the ink as an invader. Special cleaning cells of the [[@immune-system|immune system]], called macrophages, swallow the ink but can't break it down. When those cells die, new ones swallow the same ink again, so the picture stays put for decades.

text: Rangoli is a pattern drawn on the floor, usually at the entrance of a home, to welcome guests and good fortune. It is made by letting powder trickle from between your thumb and forefinger, as if you were sprinkling salt very slowly. Artists use rice flour, chalk powder, crushed stone, coloured powders or flower petals.

Designs range from a simple row of lotuses to huge, detailed circles of peacocks and lamps. Rangoli is drawn for festivals such as [[@diwali-lights|Diwali]], [[@onam-pongal|Onam and Pongal]], for weddings and new homes, and in many households every morning. Then it is swept away, and a new one is drawn.

Using chalk or white crayon, try to draw lines that curve around the dots without touching them, and see if you can make a pattern with one continuous line. myth: Rangoli is only a Diwali decoration.

Many families draw a kolam or rangoli every single day, and the tradition is tied to harvest festivals, weddings, Onam, Pongal and the cold month of Margazhi, as well as Diwali. Each region has its own name and style.

sec.t:
Almost every part of India has its own floor art. In Tamil Nadu it is the *kolam*, in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana *muggulu*, and in Karnataka *rangavalli*. In Bengal, women paint *alpana* with a paste of rice and water, using a finger or a twist of cloth. In Rajasthan, *mandana* designs are drawn in white on floors and walls coated with red earth. In Kerala, the *pookalam* at Onam is made entirely of flower petals.

The styles differ too. Some use only white lines. Others are filled with rich colours. Some show gods and animals, like the wall paintings of [[@madhubani|Madhubani]]. Others are pure [[geometry|geometry]].

In Tamil Nadu, a kolam drawn in rice flour is said to be a small act of kindness: it feeds [[@ants-world|ants]], birds and other small creatures that pass by. The doorstep is first swept and sprinkled with water, which keeps dust down and helps the flour stick.

During Margazhi, the cold month from mid-December to mid-January, kolams become bigger and more elaborate. Streets in Chennai and other towns fill with designs that spread across the road, and some neighbourhoods hold competitions. On Pongal, kolams show pots of rice boiling over, a sign of plenty.

Experienced artists draw freehand, but beginners can use tricks. Draw a chalk outline first, or use a grid of dots as a guide. Some people use stencils, or plastic shakers with holes. For bright colours, powders are often made from coloured rock dust, or from rice flour mixed with natural dyes like turmeric.

The trick is control. Pinch the powder, keep your hand close to the floor and move steadily. Lines come out even only after a lot of practice, which is why many grandmothers can draw a perfect kolam in minutes while beginners struggle. Many learners practise on paper or a slate first, before trying the doorstep.

Indian families have carried rangoli wherever they settled. In the United States, it is drawn at Diwali on doorsteps, in temples and at school celebrations, sometimes with sidewalk chalk. In Malaysia, Singapore and Mauritius, malls and town squares display giant festive rangolis. Wherever it is made, the idea stays the same. A doorstep should look welcoming, even if the pattern lasts only a day.

text: Equality is the idea that every person has the same worth and should have the same basic rights and chances, whatever their religion, [[@caste-history|caste]], race, gender, wealth or disability. Nobody is born more important than anyone else.

In practice it has several parts. Equality before the law means the same rules apply to a minister and [[@people-street-vendors|a street vendor]]. Equality of opportunity means everyone gets a fair chance at school, jobs and public life. And many people add a third idea: that a fair society should help those who started further behind.

st.reveal: Giving everyone the same thing is one kind of fairness. But if one child is much shorter, the same box may not be enough. Many people call giving help according to need "equity", and they argue about when each approach is fairer.

India's Constitution makes equality a Fundamental [[@rights-duties|Right]]. Article 14 promises everyone equality before the law. Article 15 bans discrimination by religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. Article 17 abolished untouchability, the old practice of treating some castes as "impure" and keeping them away from temples, wells and schools.

In the United States, the 14th Amendment of 1868 promised "equal protection of the laws". For almost a century, though, many states still kept Black and white Americans apart in schools, buses and restaurants.

sec.h: Water, a school and a bus seat

sec.t: For most of history, women could not vote. [[@new-zealand|New Zealand]] gave women the vote nationally in 1893, the United States in 1920, and Britain on equal terms with men only in 1928. India's Constitution gave every adult the vote from 1950, so its first general election, in 1951–52, included women from the start.

People often disagree about how to reach equality. Some say the fairest thing is to treat everyone the same and let them compete. Others say that groups held back for centuries need extra help to catch up, like reserved seats in colleges or jobs. India's system of [[@reservation-india|reservations]] for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other backward classes comes from this second view. Supporters say it has opened doors for millions. Critics argue about who should benefit and for how long. Both sides usually agree the goal is the same.

Women around the world still earn less on average than men. People with disabilities often find buildings, buses and websites built without them in mind, as you can read in [[@disabilities-inclusion|disabilities and inclusion]]. In 2018, a law came into force in Iceland requiring larger companies to prove they pay men and women equally for the same work. Each generation finds new places where the promise of equality has not yet reached, and new people willing to push for it.

text: The Red Cross is a worldwide movement that helps people in wars, disasters and other emergencies. It gives first aid, food, water, shelter and medical care, and it helps separated families find each other. It also visits prisoners of war and reminds armies of the rules of war.

It has three parts. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), based in Geneva, works mainly in wars. There are 191 national societies (2024), such as the Indian Red Cross Society and the American Red Cross, which help people in their own countries. And the International Federation links those societies together.

It is a religious symbol from the Bible

st.reveal: The founders met in Geneva and reversed the Swiss flag, a white cross on red, as a tribute. It was meant as a neutral sign of protection, though some countries later felt it looked Christian and chose the red crescent instead.

myth: The red cross is a Christian symbol.

It was chosen as the reverse of the Swiss flag, not for religious reasons. Even so, some countries saw it as Christian, which is why the red crescent and later the red crystal were added as equal emblems.

sec.t:
On 24 June 1859, armies of France and Austria fought near the village of Solferino in northern Italy. Within a day, around 40,000 soldiers were dead or wounded. A Swiss businessman named Henry Dunant happened to arrive. He found wounded men lying in fields and churches with almost no one to care for them.

Dunant organised local villagers, mostly women, to bring water, food and bandages. They helped soldiers from both sides, saying "tutti fratelli", "all are brothers". Back in Geneva, he wrote a book, *A Memory of Solferino*, published in 1862. It asked two questions. Could every country train volunteers to help the wounded in war? And could countries agree to protect those helpers?

The red cross was chosen in honour of Switzerland. But in the 1870s, during a war between Russia and the Ottoman Empire, Ottoman forces used a red crescent instead, saying the cross offended Muslim soldiers. The red crescent was officially recognised in 1929. In 2005, a third emblem, the red crystal, was added for countries that did not want to use either.

All three mean the same thing: do not attack, these people are here to help.

The Indian Red Cross Society was set up by an act of Parliament in 1920. Its national headquarters is in New Delhi, with branches across the states. It runs blood banks, trains people in [[@first-aid|first aid]] and helps after floods, [[cyclone|cyclones]] and earthquakes. Many Indian schools have Junior Red Cross groups.

The American Red Cross was founded in 1881 by Clara Barton, a nurse who had cared for soldiers in the US Civil War. Today it collects a large share of the donated blood used in American hospitals, which is why many people know it best for [[@blood-donation|blood donation]].

The ICRC follows strict principles. It is neutral, meaning it doesn't take sides in a war. It is impartial, helping people based only on need. And it is independent of governments.

That neutrality lets its workers cross front lines and visit prisons that others can't enter. It also brings criticism. During the Second World War, the ICRC knew about the Nazi camps but did not speak out publicly, a decision it has since called a failure. Henry Dunant, meanwhile, went bankrupt and was forgotten for years. A journalist found him living in a Swiss care home, and in 1901 he shared the first Nobel Peace Prize.

text: Wangari Maathai was a Kenyan scientist who started the Green Belt Movement in 1977. She did not plant millions of trees herself. She got thousands of women in villages across Kenya to do it, and paid them a little for every seedling that survived.
The trees gave the women firewood, fruit and shade, and held the [[@soil-made|soil]] in place so streams kept flowing. The work also gave women money and confidence.
The movement has planted more than 5 crore (50 million) trees. In 2004, Maathai won the [[@nobel-peace|Nobel Peace Prize]], the first African woman to do so.

st.reveal: Forests had been cleared for farms and plantations. Without trees, streams dried, soil washed away and women walked much further for firewood. Maathai's answer was simple. Plant trees.

sec.t:
Maathai was born in 1940 in Nyeri, in the green highlands of central Kenya. As a child she fetched water from a stream near a fig tree, and watched tadpoles swim in it. Years later, that stream had dried up, and she never forgot it.

She was a brilliant student. In 1960 she won a scholarship to study in the United States, one of hundreds of young Kenyans flown there in a programme called the Kennedy Airlift. Back home, in 1971, she became the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a PhD, in veterinary [[anatomy|anatomy]].

sec.h: How the Green Belt Movement worked
sec.t:
Women set up tree nurseries, collecting seeds from local trees and raising them in small pots. When the seedlings were ready, they were planted on farms, at schools and along roads. Foresters had said only experts could grow trees. Maathai said women had been growing things for thousands of years.

Each woman was paid a small sum for every tree that was still alive after a few months. That rule meant people cared for the trees long after planting.

Maathai also fought the government when it wanted to build on public green spaces. In 1989 she campaigned against a 60-storey tower planned for Uhuru Park in [[@world-nairobi|Nairobi]]. The tower was never built.

Protecting forests and speaking up for [[@democracy-what|democracy]] got her arrested and beaten more than once. She kept going, and in 2002 she was elected to Kenya's [[parliament|parliament]].

Some people were puzzled when Maathai won the Nobel Peace Prize. What did trees have to do with peace?

The Nobel Committee explained that when land is stripped bare, people compete for scarce water, firewood and farmland, and that competition can turn into conflict. Caring for the land, it said, helps prevent fights before they start. Maathai agreed. She also saw that women planting trees together learned to organise, speak up and demand fair treatment, which is how [[democracy|democracy]] grows.

The Green Belt Movement spread beyond Kenya to other African countries. In 2006 she helped launch a UN campaign that set out to plant a billion trees around the world in a single year, and it passed that goal.

Maathai liked to tell a story. A forest is on fire, and the big animals flee. A tiny hummingbird flies back and forth, dropping water on the flames one beakful at a time. When the others laugh, it says, "I am doing the best I can." She died in 2011, and the trees her movement planted are still growing in Kenya.

text: Pi Day is a celebration of [[@pi|pi]], the number you get when you divide the distance around any circle by the distance across it. Pi starts 3.14159 and its digits go on forever, never settling into a repeating pattern.

In the United States, dates are written month first, so 14 March becomes 3/14, the first three digits of pi. People mark the day with maths games, digit-reciting contests and, of course, pies. Since 2020, 14 March has also been the International Day of Mathematics, set up by UNESCO. In India, where dates are written day first, some people prefer 22 July, written 22/7, because 22 divided by 7 is close to pi.

st.prompt: How many decimal places of pi do NASA engineers use to plan spacecraft paths?
st.reveal: NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory uses 3.141592653589793, which is 15 decimal places. That is precise enough to calculate the path of a spacecraft billions of kilometres away to within a few centimetres.

myth: Pi is exactly 22/7.
22/7 is a handy shortcut, equal to about 3.1429. Pi is about 3.14159, and its digits go on forever without repeating, so no fraction can be exactly equal to it.

sec.h: A party at a science museum
sec.t:
The first Pi Day party was held in 1988 at the Exploratorium, a hands-on science museum in San Francisco. A physicist there, Larry Shaw, led staff in a circular parade and shared fruit pies. The idea spread to schools and universities.

In 2009, the US House of Representatives passed a resolution backing Pi Day. Some schools hold contests where students make paper chains with a different colour for each digit. Others serve pizza, another circle, because pies are rarer in many countries.

Indian mathematicians studied pi long ago. Around 499 CE, [[@aryabhata|Aryabhata]] wrote that a circle 20,000 units across has a circumference of about 62,832 units. That gives 3.1416, correct to four [[decimal|decimal]] places. He also hinted that this was only an approximation.

Around 1400, Madhava of Sangamagrama in Kerala found an endless series of fractions that adds up to pi. European mathematicians found similar formulas nearly 300 years later. And in the early 1900s, Srinivasa Ramanujan discovered formulas for pi so fast that computers still use ideas from them.

sec.h: How many digits do we need?
sec.t:
Not many. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory uses about 15 decimal places to plan the paths of [[@spacecraft-move|spacecraft]]. With around 40 decimal places, you could work out the distance around the whole observable universe to within the width of a single [[atom|atom]].

So why calculate more? Partly as a test for computers and their storage, and partly because people love a challenge. In December 2025, a team used a single computer running for about four months to work out about 314 trillion digits. Printed out, they would fill a library of books. Each record is double-checked with a different formula, so that no digit is wrong. Pi also turns up where there are no obvious circles. It appears in the maths of waves, swinging [[pendulum|pendulums]] and even dropped needles landing across floorboards.

Some people memorise thousands of digits. In 2015, Rajveer Meena, a student from Rajasthan, recited 70,000 digits of pi in about 10 hours, wearing a blindfold. That is listed by Guinness World Records as the most digits of pi memorised.

People use tricks to help, such as sentences where the number of letters in each word matches a digit. "How I wish I could calculate pi" gives 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2. And the strangest part? In 1897, lawmakers in the US state of Indiana almost passed a bill that gave pi a wrong, simpler value. Real [[@circles|circles]] would have ignored them completely.

text: In a group of 23 people, there's a slightly better than 50 per cent chance that at least two share a birthday. With 30 people, the chance rises to about 70 per cent. With 70 people, it's about 99.9 per cent, almost certain.

That surprises most people, because 23 seems tiny compared with 365 days. The trick is that you aren't asking whether anyone shares your birthday. You're asking whether any two people share any birthday at all. And the number of possible pairs grows very fast.

st.prompt: How many people do you need in a room for a better-than-even chance that two share a birthday?
st.reveal: Just 23 people is enough to pass 50 per cent. That's because you aren't looking for someone with your birthday, but any matching pair, and 23 people can make 253 different pairs.

d.try: In your class or with a group of at least 23 people, ask everyone to say their birthday, day and month, one by one. Keep a list and see if any two match. Try it in a few classes. About half the time you should find at least one match.
myth: You need about 183 people, half of 365, to have an even chance of a shared birthday.
That would be the number for someone to share your particular birthday, which needs about 253 people. For any two people to share any birthday, only 23 are needed.

sec.t:
In a group of 23, how many different pairs can you make? The first person can pair with 22 others. The second can pair with 21 new people, and so on. Add them up and you get 253 pairs.

Each pair has a small chance of matching, about 1 in 365. But with 253 chances, those small odds add up. It's like buying 253 lottery tickets instead of one.

Now compare that with asking whether someone in the room shares your own birthday. Then only 22 pairs include you, and the chance is only about 6 per cent.

Mathematicians find the answer by flipping the question. What's the chance that nobody shares a birthday?

The first person can have any birthday. The second must avoid that day, so has 364 out of 365 options. The third must avoid two days: 363 out of 365. Keep going for all 23 people and multiply those chances together.

The answer comes to about 49.3 per cent. So the chance that at least two do share is about 50.7 per cent. Do the same for 70 people and the "nobody shares" chance shrinks to about 0.1 per cent.

{{story:life-birthdays-world}}

In 2014, the BBC checked the squads at the football World Cup in Brazil. Each team had 23 players, the magic number.

Of the 32 squads, 16 had at least one pair of players with the same birthday. Exactly half, as [[@probability|probability]] predicts. Some squads even had two pairs.

You can test it in an Indian school too, where a class of 40 is common. With 40 students, the chance of a shared birthday is about 89 per cent.

The maths assumes every day is equally likely. In real life, they aren't. In the USA, more babies are born in September than in other months, and fewer around big holidays. Doctors often avoid scheduling planned births on holidays.

The 29th of February comes only in [[@leap-years|leap years]], so it's rare. Uneven birthdays actually make shared birthdays slightly more likely than the simple maths says.

To be completely sure two people share a birthday, you need 367 people, one more than the number of possible days, including 29 February. This idea is called the pigeonhole principle: if you have more pigeons than holes, at least two must share.

The birthday puzzle isn't just a party trick. In computing, files and passwords are often turned into short codes called hashes. Two different things might accidentally get the same code, a bit like two people sharing a birthday.

Because of the birthday effect, these clashes happen sooner than you'd guess. Security experts use the maths to decide how long codes must be, so hackers can't find matches easily. Birthday maths is quietly built into the [[@cryptography-maths|maths of secret codes]].

People get this puzzle wrong for the same reason they struggle with the [[@puzzle-monty-hall|Monty Hall puzzle]]. We think about ourselves, not about all the possible pairs. And we're bad at feeling how fast numbers grow when things combine.

At the next big party you go to, count the guests. If there are more than 23, it's more likely than not that two of them share a birthday, and they probably have no idea.

text: Most big animated films today are made with computers. Artists build characters and worlds as 3D models, a bit like digital puppets. Animators then pose those puppets frame by frame, and powerful computers turn each frame into a finished picture with light, colour and shadow.

It is slow, careful work. A 90-minute film shown at 24 frames a second needs about 1,30,000 frames. Big studios such as [[@pixar|Pixar]] and Disney in the USA, and smaller ones in India, Japan and Europe, may spend four years or more on one film.

st.prompt: In most big animated films, what is recorded first?
st.reveal: Voices usually come first, because animators shape every mouth movement and facial expression to match the words. Music and sound effects are mostly added near the end, once the pictures are finished.

The computer handles the drawing and the maths, but people decide every pose, expression and movement. A skilled animator might finish only a few seconds of film in a whole week.

sec.t:
Every film starts with a story, and the story changes many times. Artists draw thousands of quick sketches called storyboards, a bit like a comic of the whole film. These are filmed with rough voices to make a test version called a story reel.

If a joke falls flat or a scene is confusing, it is cheap to fix now and very expensive to fix later. Whole characters are sometimes cut. Then actors record the real voices, often alone in a sound booth, months or years before they see the finished film.

Animators move the rigged puppets. They set a few key poses, and the computer fills in the frames between them. The animator then adjusts those in-between frames by hand, because computers move things too smoothly and evenly.

Good animators study how real things move. They film themselves acting a scene, watch animals at the zoo and think about weight. A heavy character lands with a thump and a slow recovery. A light one bounces. This is why some animators read up on [[@gravity-fall|falling and gravity]] as much as on drawing.

Some things are too complicated to animate by hand, such as flowing hair, splashing water, fluttering clothes or a crowd of thousands. Here, software simulates the physics. When Pixar made *Monsters, Inc.*, it had to create new tools just to make Sulley's two million hairs sway naturally.

Finally comes rendering, when computers work out the colour of every [[@pixels|pixel]] in every frame. A single frame can take hours. Studios use render farms, rooms full of thousands of linked computers working day and night. This is why the [[@computers-how|computers]] at a big studio are among the busiest anywhere.

India has a large animation industry. Studios in cities such as Mumbai, Hyderabad and Bengaluru do work for American and European films and series. Green Gold Animation in Hyderabad created *[[@chhota-bheem|Chhota Bheem]]*, first shown in 2008, which became one of India's most popular children's cartoons.

Hand-drawn and stop-motion films have not disappeared either. Some directors still prefer the look of paint or clay, and audiences keep watching. The tools have changed, but the old idea is the same: still pictures, shown fast enough, start to breathe.

text: The Indian Premier League, or IPL, is a professional cricket competition that began in 2008. City-based teams play Twenty20 matches, with 20 overs a side, over about two months each spring. It mixes Indian players with stars from around the world.

The IPL changed cricket in three big ways. It brought huge amounts of money into the game. It made batting more daring, as players invented new shots. And it inspired copycat leagues from Australia to the United States.

sec.t:
In 2007 India won the first T20 [[@cricket-world-cups|World Cup]] in South Africa. Fans went wild for the short, fast format. The Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) quickly launched a league for it.

The first match was played on 18 April 2008 at the [[@stadiums|Chinnaswamy Stadium]] in [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]]. Brendon McCullum of New Zealand hit 158 not out from 73 balls for Kolkata Knight Riders. Crowds and [[@television-invented|television]] audiences were enormous from the start.

The league has had to move house twice. In 2009 it was played in South Africa because India was holding a general election. In 2020, during the COVID-19 [[pandemic|pandemic]], it moved to the United Arab Emirates and was played in mostly empty stadiums.

The IPL's broadcast rights for 2023 to 2027 were sold for about ₹48,000 crore. That money pays players, builds facilities and funds Indian cricket. Most fans now watch on phones as well as television, through [[@streaming|streaming]] apps.

Players from countries with smaller cricket budgets can earn more in two months of IPL than in years of playing at home. That has changed what young cricketers everywhere dream about.

T20 cricket rewards risk. IPL batters began to play ramps over the wicketkeeper, reverse sweeps and switch hits, shots once seen as tricks. Team totals rose steadily. In 2024 Sunrisers Hyderabad scored 287 for 3 against Royal Challengers Bengaluru, the highest total in IPL history at the time.

Bowlers fought back with yorkers, slower balls and knuckle balls. Teams now use [[@sports-science|data analysts]] to plan which bowler should face which batter.

Fans love the IPL's speed, music and drama. It has given hundreds of Indian players a professional living and found stars such as Jasprit Bumrah. Royal Challengers Bengaluru, one of the original teams, finally won its first title in 2025 after 17 years of trying, and won again in 2026.

It has also faced criticism. In 2013 a spot-fixing scandal led to two teams being suspended for two seasons. Some players and former cricketers worry that the money pulls talent away from [[@test-cricket|Test cricket]] and crowds the calendar. Others argue that the IPL has brought millions of new fans to cricket in all its forms. Even [[@kabaddi|kabaddi]] and [[@kho-kho|kho-kho]] have copied its idea, with city teams and prime-time matches of their own.

text: Marbles have lasted because they are cheap, small and endlessly flexible. A pocket of little balls and a patch of flat ground are enough for dozens of games. You can flick them into a hole, knock other marbles out of a ring, trade them or simply admire the swirls of colour inside.

Children in many ancient societies played with small round stones, clay balls or nuts. Spinning tops are almost as old. Both toys use simple physics that feels like magic: a flick that sends a marble rolling true, a twist that makes a top stand on its point. Each generation teaches the next, often without any adult involved.

st.prompt: Why does a spinning top stay upright, but fall over as soon as it stops?

options.t: Spinning makes it resist tipping over
Air pushes up on it while it spins
The floor grips it more tightly when it spins

st.reveal: A fast-spinning object resists changes to the direction it points, an effect physicists call angular momentum. As friction slows the top, it starts to wobble, and finally falls.

sec.t:
Small clay and stone balls have been found at many ancient sites, including the [[@indus-cities|Indus cities]] of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, more than 4,000 years old. [[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] can't always be sure what they were for, but many were probably used in games.

In ancient Rome, children played similar games with nuts, rolling them at targets or into holes. When Romans said someone had "left the nuts behind", they meant that person had grown up. It's one of the oldest clues that [[@toys-history|toys]] like these marked childhood.

In India, marbles are called kanche, goli or other local names, and games are played in lanes and school grounds everywhere. One common game has players flicking their marble with a bent finger at others scattered on the ground, winning any they hit.

In the USA, a classic game is ringer. Thirteen marbles are set out in a cross inside a ring about 3 metres across, and players kneel at the edge and shoot to knock them out. The English phrase "playing for keeps" comes from marble games where winners kept the marbles they won. Many children carry one favourite, heavier marble, the shooter, which they never risk.

A glass marble also seals the famous goli soda bottle. In 1872 an English inventor, Hiram Codd, designed a bottle where the fizz pushes a marble up against a rubber ring, closing the neck. You press the marble down to open it. Codd bottles vanished from most countries, but they're still filled and sold in parts of India and Japan.

Spinning tops have been made from clay, wood, bone and plastic for thousands of years. In India, wooden tops called lattu in Hindi and bambaram in Tamil are wound with a string and thrown so they land spinning. Karnataka's [[@channapatna-toys|Channapatna toys]] include brightly lacquered tops.

A spinning top stays up because of angular momentum: a spinning object resists tipping. [[friction|Friction]] from the floor and air slowly steals its spin. Only a tiny point touches the ground, which keeps that friction low. Tops with more weight near the rim tend to spin longer, for the same reason a heavy potter's wheel keeps turning after a push. In the 2000s, Japanese battle tops called Beyblades made the old toy a global craze. In the USA, a National Marbles Tournament for young players has been held almost every year since 1922. The toys change shape. The urge to flick and spin does not.

People love him for several reasons. His screen style is like nobody else's. His life story, from bus conductor to superstar, feels like one of his own films. And off screen he seems humble and ordinary, which makes fans feel he is one of them.

sec.h: From bus tickets to the big screen
sec.t:
He was born Shivaji Rao Gaekwad on 12 December 1950 in Bengaluru, into a Marathi family of modest means. His mother died when he was a boy. As a young man he did odd jobs, including carpentry and carrying loads, and then worked as a conductor on city buses.

He loved acting in amateur plays, often in Kannada plays based on stories from the epics. Friends encouraged him to join the Madras Film Institute in Chennai. There, the director K. Balachander noticed him and gave him a small role in *Apoorva Raagangal* in 1975. Balachander also gave him his screen name.

A new Rajinikanth film in Tamil Nadu feels like a festival. Fans gather before dawn for the first show, put up giant cut-outs of him and set off firecrackers. When *Kabali* came out in 2016, some companies in Chennai and Bengaluru gave their staff the day off.

His fame travelled far beyond India. *Muthu* was released in Japan in 1998 and became a surprise hit there. Many of his films are [[@dubbing-subtitles|dubbed]] into Telugu, Hindi and other languages, so fans across the country can follow them.

What surprises many people is how plain he looks in real life. He often appears in public without his screen wig or makeup, in a simple white shirt. He is known for being polite to everyone on set, from fellow stars to the crew who carry the lights. He has spoken openly about his early struggles and regularly travels to the Himalayas for spiritual retreats.

In 2020, he announced plans to start a political party, then dropped them, saying his health came first. Supporters were disappointed, and others said it was the right choice. Either way, his fans stayed loyal.

The Government of India gave him the Padma Bhushan in 2000 and the Padma Vibhushan in 2016. He received the Dadasaheb Phalke Award, India's highest film honour, named after the [[@dadasaheb-phalke|father of Indian cinema]], for 2019.

He is also the hero of countless internet jokes, which claim he can do impossible things, like counting to infinity twice. The jokes are made with affection, and they spread through emails and websites in the late 2000s, long before most people had smartphones. In a way, they are another sign of how much people across [[@cinema-south|South Indian cinema]] and beyond enjoy him.

text: Motion sickness happens when your senses send your brain messages that don't match. Your inner ear has a balance system that feels every turn, bump and swing of the car. But if you're looking at a phone or a book, your eyes tell your brain that you're sitting still.

The brain gets confused by this disagreement. Scientists aren't fully sure why, but the confusion sets off feelings of sickness: a sweaty face, yawning, a headache, a queasy stomach and sometimes vomiting. It can happen in cars, buses, boats, planes, on fairground rides and even while playing video games. Children between about 2 and 12 get it most.

sec.t:
Deep inside each ear, beyond the parts that hear, is the vestibular system. It has three tiny curved tubes filled with fluid, set at different angles. When your head turns, the fluid lags behind and bends tiny hair-like [[sensor|sensors]]. They tell your brain which way you're turning.

Two small sacs nearby contain tiny crystals that shift when you speed up, slow down or tilt. Together, these parts work like a motion sensor in a phone. Your brain combines their messages with what your eyes see and what your muscles and joints feel. Normally they all agree, and you barely notice your sense of balance at all.

Winding mountain roads are hard on sensitive stomachs. Many Indian families know the feeling on [[@himachal|hill roads]] in Himachal, the ghat roads up to Ooty or the twisting climb to Darjeeling. The constant left-right swing of hairpin bends is a strong trigger.

At sea, the slow up-and-down rolling of a boat is the classic cause. Many sailors feel sick for the first few days, then their brains adjust. When they get back on land, some feel as if the ground is still moving.

[[@astronaut-life|Astronauts]] get a version called space sickness. In space there's no "down", so the inner ear gives strange signals. More than half of astronauts feel ill during their first few days, before their brains adapt.

[[@vr-ar|Virtual reality]] can cause the opposite problem. Your eyes see you flying or running, but your inner ear says you're standing still. That mismatch makes some people feel just as sick as in a car.

Looking out at the horizon helps, because it lets your eyes see the same movement your ears feel. Sitting where the motion is smallest helps too: in the middle of a boat, over the wing of a plane, or facing forwards in a car or train. Fresh air, small light meals before travelling and not reading on the move can all make a difference.

Some people find that [[@ginger-garlic|ginger]] settles their stomach, and there's some evidence it helps a little. Doctors can suggest medicines for long trips, and it's best to ask a doctor or pharmacist before giving any to a child. Most children grow out of travel sickness as they get older.

There are also small tricks people swear by. Some listen to music or close their eyes. Others count telephone poles out of the window, which keeps their eyes on the real movement outside. On long bus journeys, sitting near the front, where the swing is smaller, can make the trip far easier.

text: In the 1860s, the strongest explosive known was nitroglycerine, an oily liquid so jumpy that a sharp knock could set it off. Alfred Nobel, a Swedish chemist and businessman, found a way to tame it. He soaked the liquid into kieselguhr, a light, crumbly earth, and packed the paste into paper tubes. In 1867, he patented it as dynamite, from the Greek word for power.

Dynamite was much safer to carry and handle, and it only exploded when set off by a small detonator, which Nobel had also invented. It made him enormously rich, and he left most of his fortune to fund the Nobel Prizes.

st.prompt: Nobel made liquid nitroglycerine safer by soaking it into something. What was it?

options.t: A crumbly earth made of the tiny fossil shells of algae

st.reveal: Kieselguhr is made of the glassy shells of diatoms, microscopic algae that lived long ago. It is full of tiny holes and soaks up liquid like a sponge, turning a jumpy liquid into a paste that could be shaped into sticks.

n.certNote: A popular story says Nobel discovered dynamite when nitroglycerine leaked into packing material by accident. Nobel himself said it came from deliberate experiments, and historians generally side with him.
