sec.h: A liquid that scared its inventor
sec.t:
Nitroglycerine was first made in 1847 by an Italian chemist, Ascanio Sobrero. He was badly hurt by an explosion and was so worried about its dangers that he warned people against using it. A little nitroglycerine contains enough energy to shatter rock, but it could also blow up from heat, shaking or even a drop on the floor.

Nobel saw its power for mining and building. Back then, miners still broke rock with gunpowder, picks and muscle, and a single tunnel could take decades. His family had a factory, and he set out to make the liquid useful.

In 1864, an explosion at the Nobel family's workshop in Stockholm killed five people, including Alfred's younger brother Emil. The city banned nitroglycerine experiments within its limits. Nobel moved his work to a barge on a lake outside the city.

Elsewhere, factories and ships carrying nitroglycerine blew up. Some countries banned it altogether, and many shipping companies refused to carry it. Nobel badly needed a safer form.

Dynamite changed building almost overnight. Miners used it to reach deeper ores. Railway builders used it to blast [[@tunnels|tunnels]], like the 15 km Gotthard tunnel through the Swiss Alps, finished in 1882. It cut paths for roads, harbours and the Panama Canal.

It also went to war, and that troubled many people. Nobel made other explosives too, and owned factories in many countries. He held more than 350 patents, from synthetic rubber to artificial silk.

A famous story says that in 1888, when Nobel's brother Ludvig died, a French newspaper wrongly printed Alfred's obituary and called him a "merchant of death". Historians are not sure the article ever existed in that form, but the story is often used to explain what Nobel did next.

When he died in 1896, his will left most of his fortune to fund yearly prizes for physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace. The first were awarded in 1901. Since then, winners have included [[@marie-curie|Marie Curie]], twice, and Indian winners from Rabindranath Tagore to C. V. Raman. Peacemakers receive the [[@nobel-peace|Nobel Peace Prize]] in Oslo.

The oddest twist is medical. Tiny doses of nitroglycerine widen blood vessels, and it is still used to ease chest pain from a struggling [[@heart-health|heart]]. Late in life, Nobel's own doctors prescribed it to him.

text: For thousands of years, a message could only travel as fast as a runner, a horse, a ship or a pigeon. Then, in the 1840s, the electric [[@telegraph|telegraph]] sent words along wires in seconds, using dots and dashes called Morse code.

After that, each new invention made messages faster, cheaper and more personal. The telephone carried voices. Radio went without wires. Computers brought email. Mobile phones brought text messages. Finally, apps like WhatsApp let anyone send words, photos, videos and voice notes to the other side of the world for almost nothing. The journey took about 170 years.

st.reveal: Engineer Neil Papworth typed "Merry Christmas" on a computer and sent it to a phone in Britain. Phones at the time couldn't type messages, so nobody could reply.

myth: Nobody uses Morse code any more.
Ships and armies have mostly switched to other systems, but amateur radio operators around the world still send Morse every day. It can get through when voice signals are too weak.

sec.t:
In 1844 the American inventor Samuel Morse sent a message on a wire from Washington to Baltimore, about 60 km away. It read "What hath God wrought". An operator tapped a key, sending short and long pulses of electricity. At the other end, a clicking machine marked them on paper.

Each letter had its own pattern of short and long signals. E, the most common letter in English, got a single dot. Q, a rare one, got dash-dash-dot-dash. [[@codes-morse|Morse code]] let one wire carry any words at all, in any language written in the right letters.

Later, Morse went wireless, sent by radio from ships. Its distress call, SOS, is three dots, three dashes and three dots. It was chosen because it is easy to send and recognise, not because the letters stand for words. When the Titanic sank in 1912, its radio operators sent SOS along with an older call, CQD.

The telephone, patented in 1876, let people talk instead of tap. By the 1900s, cities had switchboards where operators connected calls by hand. In 1971 an engineer named Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between computers, choosing the @ sign to separate the person from the machine.

Mobile phones came next. In 1992, the first SMS was sent in Britain. SMS messages were limited to 160 characters, which is why people invented short forms like "gr8" and "c u". In India, by the 2000s, texting had become a cheap way for families to keep in touch. Twitter, now called X, launched in 2006 with a 140-character limit on posts, an idea borrowed from text messages.

WhatsApp was launched in 2009 by two former Yahoo engineers. It used the internet instead of the phone company's text system, so messages cost almost nothing, even abroad. By 2025 it had more than 3 billion monthly users, and India had more than any other country.

Since 2016, WhatsApp messages have been protected by end-to-end [[@encryption|encryption]], so only the sender and receiver can read them. Messaging is now so fast that false rumours can spread too, and some countries limit how often a message can be forwarded. A telegram once took hours and cost money for every word. Now a family can share a birthday video between Bengaluru and Boston before the candles finish burning.

text: A prosthetic is an artificial body part, and a "bionic" one has motors and electronics. Many bionic arms are myoelectric: they read the tiny electrical signals your [[@muscles|muscles]] make when you tighten them. Someone who has lost a hand still has muscles in their forearm. When they try to close the hand, those muscles twitch, and [[sensor|sensors]] resting on the skin inside the socket pick up the signal.

A small computer turns that signal into a command, and motors in the hand open or close the fingers. Bionic legs work differently. They use sensors to feel the ground and microprocessors to adjust the [[@joints|knee or ankle]] many times a second, so walking downhill or up stairs feels steadier.

options.t: Sensors on the skin pick up electrical signals when the person tightens muscles in their arm

st.reveal: When you tighten a muscle, it makes a tiny electrical signal. Sensors inside the socket of a bionic arm pick this up through the skin, and a small computer turns it into motor movements in the hand.

Modern prosthetics can do a lot, but none yet match a natural limb's feeling, speed and control. Most users can't feel what their prosthetic hand touches. Running blades help athletes, but scientists still debate whether they give any advantage.

sec.h: Thousands of years of spare parts
sec.t:
People have been making replacement body parts for a very long time. A wooden toe with leather straps, found on the foot of an Egyptian woman's mummy, is about 3,000 years old and shows signs of wear, so it was probably used for walking. Another, made of linen, glue and plaster, is in the British Museum. Ancient [[@ancient-egypt|Egyptians]] cared about walking well, and they cared about being buried whole.

For most of history, artificial legs were wooden pegs and artificial hands were hooks. Wars, which left many soldiers injured, pushed inventors to make better ones, with joints, [[@springs|springs]] and straps.

Look at sprinters at the [[@paralympics|Paralympics]] and you'll see curved blades instead of feet. They are made of carbon fibre, a light, strong material that bends like a spring as the runner lands and springs back as they push off.

They're designed for running only. Standing still on them is wobbly, so athletes switch to a different leg for walking. Scientists still debate whether blades give an advantage over natural legs or not, and sports bodies decide case by case.

The hardest problem is feeling. Your real hand sends a stream of messages up your [[@nervous-system|nerves]], telling your brain how hard you are gripping and whether something is slipping. Most prosthetic hands send nothing back, so users have to watch what they are doing.

Researchers are testing ways to fix this. In one approach, surgeons move nerves that once served the lost hand into other muscles, giving clearer signals to control a bionic arm. In another, tiny electrodes on the remaining [[nerve|nerves]] send buzzes back to [[@brain-works|the brain]] when the hand's fingertips touch something. Some people can now tell a soft grape from a hard ball with their eyes closed.

A top bionic arm can cost as much as a car. To bring costs down, volunteers and small companies use [[@3d-printing|3D printers]] to make simple [[@plastic-made|plastic]] hands, especially for children, who outgrow them quickly. A child can get a new hand in a favourite colour, or one that looks like a superhero's, for far less than the price of a standard prosthetic.

text: Early people made stone tools by hitting one stone with another. A hard, rounded hammerstone was struck against the edge of a stone such as flint, quartzite or obsidian. A thin, sharp flake broke off. That flake could cut meat, scrape hides or whittle wood.

This way of shaping stone is called knapping. The oldest widely accepted tools, from Ethiopia, are about 2.6 million years old. They were probably made by early members of our human family, long before our own [[species|species]] appeared. Over time, toolmakers learned to shape stones into neat, balanced hand [[axis|axes]], then tiny blades that could be fixed onto spears and arrows.

st.reveal: Flint, chert and obsidian are hard and break in smooth, shell-shaped curves, leaving razor-thin edges. Sandstone falls apart into grains, and marble is too soft. Toolmakers sometimes carried good stone for many kilometres.

Natural History Museum (London), Stone tools.
n.certNote: Most experts agree that stone tools go back at least 2.6 million years. Older finds from Kenya, dated to about 3.3 million years, are accepted by many scientists but questioned by some, and the age of India's oldest tools is still being studied.

d.try: Collect a few pebbles from a garden or riverbank and sort them by how they feel. Which are gritty, which are smooth, which are heavy for their size? Early toolmakers did this kind of sorting by eye and hand. Don't try to break stones yourself, because flying chips can hurt your eyes.
myth: Cave people just picked up any rock and used it as a tool.
Making a good stone tool takes skill and planning. Toolmakers chose the right stone, struck it at the right angle and shaped it in a set order. Modern experts who try it need months of practice.
facts: Attirampakkam near Chennai, about 1.5 million years

sec.t:
Not every stone will do. The best ones are hard and glassy inside, with no grain. When struck, they break in a smooth curve, like a chip off a thick glass bottle. Flint, chert, quartzite and obsidian all work well.

In India, many early tools are made of quartzite, which is common in riverbeds. In parts of Africa and the Middle East, flint was the favourite. Knowing your [[@rocks-types|rocks]] mattered. [[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] have found tools made from stone that came from quarries many kilometres away, so people must have carried good stone with them.

A skilled knapper holds the core stone firmly and hits near its edge with a hammerstone at a sharp angle. Each blow knocks off a flake. By turning the core and striking again and again, the knapper shapes it step by step.

Later toolmakers also used softer hammers of bone, [[antler|antler]] or wood, which gave more control. They pressed tiny flakes off with a pointed antler tip to sharpen edges. Modern researchers who learn knapping say it takes months of practice, and plenty of cut fingers, to make even a rough hand axe. That tells us early humans had to plan, teach and learn.

On 30 May 1863, the [[geologist|geologist]] Robert Bruce Foote found a stone hand axe at Pallavaram, near what is now Chennai. It was one of the first such tools recognised in India, and it showed that [[@early-humans-india|early humans]] had lived there in the deep past.

Nearby, at Attirampakkam, scientists later dated hand axes to around 1.5 million years ago. Some of that dating is still being checked, but it suggests toolmakers reached India surprisingly early.

Bones rot away, but stone lasts. Scattered tools are often the only sign that people once lived in a valley or along a river. By studying how the flakes were struck, [[@archaeology|archaeologists]] can work out whether a person was right-handed, what they were cutting and even how many steps they planned ahead.

The [[@stone-age|Stone Age]] did not end because people ran out of stones. It slowly faded as people learned to smelt copper and bronze, a few thousand years ago. Even then, sharp stone blades stayed in use for a long time in many places.

text: The northernmost proper town on Earth is Longyearbyen, on the island of Spitsbergen in the Svalbard group, which belongs to Norway. It sits at about 78 degrees north, roughly 1,300 km from the North Pole. That is closer to the Pole than Delhi is to Bengaluru.

About 2,500 people lived in Longyearbyen and nearby Ny-Ålesund in 2026. Longyearbyen has a school, a university centre, a supermarket, a church and a cinema. A few research bases and military camps sit further north, but nobody would call them towns.

st.reveal: Cats are banned in Svalbard to protect the Arctic birds that nest there. Dogs are allowed, and many people keep sled dogs.

d.try: Shine a torch on a globe, or a ball with a dot drawn high up near the top. Tilt the ball a little and turn it slowly. Watch how the dot stays in light all the way round when the top leans towards the torch, and in darkness when it leans away.
myth: It is against the law to die in Longyearbyen.

There is no such law. The graveyard stopped taking burials around 1950 because the frozen ground stops bodies decaying. People who are very ill or very old are usually moved to mainland Norway, where there are proper hospitals.
facts: about late April to late August

sec.t:
Because of the tilt of the Earth, the far north has the strangest [[@seasons-why|seasons]] on the planet. From about late October to mid-February, the Sun never climbs above the horizon. For weeks in the middle of winter, it is dark even at noon.

Then it flips. From late April to late August the Sun never sets. Children play football at midnight in bright light, and people hang thick curtains or tape foil over windows so they can sleep. Clocks still say it's night, but the sky never agrees.

In the long dark, the sky often lights up with the green curtains of the [[@aurora|aurora]].

{{story:aurora}}

sec.h: Polar bears and a rifle rule
sec.t:
Polar bears roam the sea ice and coasts all around Svalbard. A hungry bear can walk into town looking for food, so anyone leaving the settled area must carry a way to scare one off, and usually a rifle too. Signs at the edge of town show a polar bear in a red triangle.

Shops and banks ask customers to leave their rifles at the door. Schoolchildren learn what to do if they ever meet a bear, the way children in Kerala might learn about snakes. Cats are not allowed at all. The ban protects the seabirds that nest on the cliffs every summer.

Below a thin top layer, the ground in Longyearbyen stays frozen all year. This is called [[permafrost|permafrost]]. Houses stand on wooden or metal poles so their warmth doesn't melt the soil beneath them.

The cold has an odd side effect. In the old graveyard, bodies from the 1918 flu outbreak barely decayed. Scientists even took samples to study that virus. Burials stopped there around 1950.

Even food arrives the hard way. Almost nothing grows on Svalbard, so fruit, vegetables and milk come by ship or plane from mainland Norway. Coal mining built the town in 1906, started by an American businessman named John Munro Longyear. That is where the name comes from: Longyear's town.

The permafrost is now warming, and in 2015 an avalanche off the mountain destroyed several homes. Svalbard is warming faster than almost anywhere on Earth.

sec.h: A vault for the world's seeds
sec.t: Dug into a mountain just outside town is the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, opened in 2008. It holds more than a million packets of seeds from almost every country, including India, kept frozen at minus 18°C. It is a backup copy of the world's crops in case disaster strikes a seed bank somewhere else.

sec.h: Why India has a home here
sec.t:
In 1920, many countries signed a [[treaty|treaty]] about Svalbard. It lets citizens of the signing countries live and work there, and India is one of them. In 2008, India opened Himadri, a research station at Ny-Ålesund, about 100 km north of Longyearbyen. Indian scientists there study [[glacier|glaciers]], the air and how the Arctic affects the [[@monsoon|monsoon]].

So the northernmost town in the world has a small Indian connection. For the same science in the far south, India runs bases on the ice of Antarctica, and those are even colder.

text: The Red Fort is a huge fortified palace in Old [[@delhi|Delhi]], built by the [[@mughals|Mughal]] emperor Shah Jahan between 1639 and 1648. Its massive walls of red sandstone stretch about 2.4 kilometres around, enclosing halls, gardens, mosques and private apartments. In its day it was called Qila-e-Mubarak, the Blessed Fort.

For about two centuries it was the home of the Mughal emperors. Today it is a symbol of the Indian nation. Every Independence Day, the Prime Minister raises the national flag on its ramparts and speaks to the country. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007.

sec.h: A new capital for an emperor
sec.t:
Shah Jahan, the emperor who built the [[@taj-mahal|Taj Mahal]] at Agra, decided to move his capital to Delhi. He built a whole new walled city there, called Shahjahanabad, with the Red Fort at its heart beside the Yamuna river. The architect is believed to be Ustad Ahmad Lahori, who is also linked to the Taj Mahal.

The fort took about nine years to build. Its two main gates are the Lahori Gate, facing Lahore, and the Delhi Gate. Through the Lahori Gate, visitors entered a covered market street called the Chatta Chowk, where merchants sold silks, jewellery and fine goods to the court.

sec.h: Halls of public and private audience

sec.t:
After Shah Jahan, the Mughal [[empire|empire]] slowly weakened. In 1739, the Persian ruler Nadir Shah invaded, looted Delhi and carried off the Peacock Throne. Later, Maratha and other armies fought for control of the city.

In 1857, Indian soldiers rebelled against the British East India Company and marched to Delhi, where they declared the old emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, their leader. After the [[@revolt-1857|revolt of 1857]] was crushed, the British put him on trial inside the Red Fort and sent him into exile in Rangoon. They then knocked down many of the fort's buildings and built army barracks in their place.

sec.h: A trial that stirred a nation
sec.t:
In 1945 and 1946, the British put three officers of the [[@subhas-bose|Indian National Army]], which had fought alongside Japan under Subhas Chandra Bose, on trial in the Red Fort. The three were a Hindu, a Muslim and a Sikh. People across India protested in their support, and the trials became a rallying point in the last years of British rule.

On 16 August 1947, the day after independence, Jawaharlal Nehru raised the tricolour at the Red Fort. The fort that had been a symbol of empire became a symbol of a free country.

Every 15 August, crowds of schoolchildren, soldiers, officials and guests gather at the Red Fort before dawn. The Prime Minister arrives, inspects a guard of honour, unfurls the flag from the ramparts above the Lahori Gate and gives a speech broadcast across India. Families watch on television, and kites fill the Delhi sky.

The Red Fort is open to visitors most days. You can walk through the Lahori Gate, along Chatta Chowk and past the marble halls. In the evening, a sound-and-light show tells its story. Like the [[@qutub-minar|Qutub Minar]], a short drive away, it lets you stand in the same spaces as rulers from centuries ago.

text: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland is a children's book written by Lewis Carroll and published in England in 1865. A girl called Alice follows a white rabbit with a pocket watch down a hole and lands in a strange world. She shrinks and grows, attends a tea party that never ends, and plays croquet with flamingos as mallets.

It is still loved because it was one of the first famous children's books that didn't try to teach a lesson. It is silly, clever and sometimes a little scary. The jokes work for children and for adults, and the dream-like world lets readers find their own meanings.

st.prompt: What was Lewis Carroll's day job?
st.reveal: Charles Dodgson taught mathematics at Christ Church, a college of Oxford University, for most of his life. He wrote books on logic and geometry under his real name, and used "Lewis Carroll" for his stories and poems.

sec.h: A story told on a river
sec.t:
On 4 July 1862, Charles Dodgson, a young maths teacher at Christ Church, Oxford, went rowing on the River Thames. With him were a friend and three sisters: Lorina, Alice and Edith Liddell. Their father was the head of his college. To pass the time, Dodgson invented a story about a girl called Alice.

Ten-year-old Alice Liddell asked him to write it down. He did, by hand, adding his own drawings, and gave it to her as a gift called Alice's Adventures Under Ground. That handmade book is now kept at the British Library in London. Dodgson then expanded the story and hired the artist John Tenniel, whose drawings are still the ones most people picture.

Dodgson was a mathematician who loved games, codes and [[@puzzles-logic|logic puzzles]]. Wonderland is full of them. Characters take words literally, argue in circles and follow rules that make no sense. The Duchess finds a moral in everything, which is Carroll poking fun at the preachy children's books of his day.

At the Mad Tea-Party the Hatter asks, "Why is a raven like a writing-desk?" Alice gives up, and the Hatter admits he has no idea either. Readers sent Carroll so many guesses that he later suggested an answer of his own. [[@riddles|Riddle]] lovers still argue about better ones.

sec.h: Words that went into the dictionary

sec.t:
The book has been translated into well over a hundred languages, including [[@hindi-language|Hindi]], Tamil and Bengali. [[@translation|Translators]] have a hard job. Many of the jokes are [[@words-puns|puns]] that only work in English, so they often invent new jokes in their own language.

Alice has also been turned into countless plays, ballets, comics and films. Walt Disney's [[@animation-studios|animated]] version came out in 1951 and gave many people their picture of a blue-dressed Alice.

Alice Liddell grew up, married and had children. In 1932, aged 80, she travelled to New York to celebrate the hundredth anniversary of Dodgson's birth, and she received an honorary degree from Columbia University. The girl in the boat had become one of the most famous children in literature.

text: The Bengal Renaissance was a burst of new ideas in Bengal, especially in [[@kolkata|Calcutta]], from about 1800 to the 1920s. Writers, reformers, teachers and scientists questioned old customs, started schools and newspapers, and created modern [[@bengali-language|Bengali]] literature.

The name borrows from the European [[@renaissance|Renaissance]], when Italy rediscovered old learning and made new art. Bengal's version mixed ideas from Indian tradition and from Western books that arrived with British rule. Not everyone agrees the name fits, but the change was real.

st.prompt: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar is best remembered for campaigning to let which group remarry?
st.reveal: In the 1850s many Hindu widows, some of them only children, were forbidden to remarry. Vidyasagar gathered support and old Sanskrit texts to argue against this, and the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act was passed in 1856.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ram Mohan Roy; Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar; Brahmo Samaj.
Kopf D. (1969) British Orientalism and the Bengal Renaissance. University of California Press.
Sarkar S. (1985) A Critique of Colonial India. Papyrus, Calcutta.
n.certNote: Historians agree that 19th-century Bengal saw a burst of new ideas. They argue over the word renaissance, because the movement mostly involved a small, educated, upper-caste elite in Calcutta and grew up under colonial rule.

sec.t:
Calcutta was the capital of British India until 1911 and the headquarters of the [[@east-india-company|East India Company]]. It had printing presses, colleges and a new class of educated Bengalis who worked as clerks, [[@jobs-lawyer|lawyers]] and teachers. They were called the bhadralok, meaning "gentle folk".

Hindu College, founded in 1817, taught science and English literature. Its students argued loudly about religion, caste and freedom. Bengali, once used mainly for religious songs and poems, became a language for essays, novels and plays. The first Bengali newspapers appeared around 1818, and [[@raja-ram-mohan-roy|Ram Mohan Roy]] soon started journals of his own in Bengali and Persian.

Writers created new kinds of Bengali literature. Michael Madhusudan Dutt brought blank verse into Bengali poetry. Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote novels, including Anandamath (1882), which contains the song "Vande Mataram", later India's national song.

Then came Rabindranath [[@tagore|Tagore]], who wrote poems, songs, stories and plays. In 1913 he became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. His songs became the national [[@anthems|anthems]] of both India and [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]].

The ideas spread beyond literature. Jagadish Chandra Bose studied [[@radio-waves|radio waves]] and plant responses. Satyendra Nath Bose's work in 1924 gave his name to a whole family of particles, the bosons. [[@swami-vivekananda|Swami Vivekananda]], a Calcutta graduate, spoke at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893, and many Americans heard about Indian [[philosophy|philosophy]] for the first time.

In 1886 Kadambini Ganguly became one of the first Indian women qualified in Western medicine. Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain wrote "Sultana's Dream" (1905), a short story about a land run by women, and opened a school for Muslim girls in Calcutta.

Historians point out that most of these changes reached a small group of mostly upper-caste, urban Hindu men. Peasants, many Muslims and most women were left out at first. Some argue the movement depended too much on British ideas, while others say Bengalis made those ideas their own. Others note that reformers in Maharashtra, Punjab and the Tamil country were questioning caste and custom at about the same time, so Bengal was far from alone.

Whatever the label, its schools, newspapers and debates helped prepare the ground for India's [[@freedom-struggle|freedom struggle]]. The arguments of that century can still be heard in Indian politics today.

text: Science fiction is storytelling that asks "what if?" about science and technology. What if we could travel through time? What if robots could think? What if we met life on another planet? The story then follows that idea to see what might happen to ordinary people.
It isn't the same as fantasy. Fantasy uses magic and doesn't need to explain itself. Science fiction usually tries to stay within what science might one day allow, even when it bends the rules.
Its worlds can be far in the future, on distant planets or in a slightly strange version of today. Many of the best stories are less about machines than about the humans using them.

sec.h: A monster and a summer storm
sec.t:
Many people call *Frankenstein*, by the English writer Mary Shelley, the first modern science fiction novel. She began it at 18, during a cold, rainy summer in Switzerland in 1816, after her friends challenged each other to write ghost stories. It was published in 1818.

Its scientist, Victor Frankenstein, uses electricity and chemistry to bring a creature to life, then abandons it. The book asks a question that still matters: are inventors responsible for what they create?

Later in the 1800s, the French writer [[@jules-verne|Jules Verne]] sent readers under the sea and to the Moon. In England, H. G. Wells wrote *The Time Machine* in 1895 and *The War of the Worlds*, about a Martian invasion, in 1898.

India's story starts early too. In 1896, the scientist Jagadish Chandra Bose wrote a short Bengali tale about stopping a [[cyclone|cyclone]] with a bottle of hair oil, which calmed the waves. It's often counted among the first science fiction stories in an Indian language.

In 1905, Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain wrote *Sultana's Dream*, in English. In her imagined Ladyland, women run the country, collect energy from the Sun and travel by flying cars, while men stay at home. It was both science fiction and a sharp joke about how women were treated.

Later, [[@satyajit-ray-stories|Satyajit Ray]] wrote about Professor Shonku, a forgetful inventor who travels the world with his cat.

{{story:alien-life}}

The term "science fiction" became popular through American magazines in the 1920s and 1930s, especially those run by the editor Hugo Gernsback. The world's top science fiction prizes, the Hugo Awards, are named after him.

Writers in those magazines dreamed up space travel, death rays and thinking machines. Isaac Asimov wrote stories about [[@robots|robots]] obeying "Three Laws", the first being that a robot may not harm a human. Engineers working on real robots and AI still argue about those laws.

Sometimes writers do guess well. In 1945, the British writer Arthur C. Clarke published an article describing satellites placed high above the [[equator|equator]], where they would circle at the same speed Earth turns. Each would seem to hang in one spot, beaming radio and TV signals. Today, such [[@satellites-help|satellites]] carry television and weather data around the world.

Other guesses missed. Many old stories gave us flying cars and robot butlers by the year 2000, but nobody predicted that everyone would carry a phone with the world's knowledge in their pocket.

Science fiction is now huge in films, TV shows, comics and games, from *[[@future-teleport|Star Trek]]* and *Star Wars* to Indian films like *Koi... Mil Gaya*, about a boy who befriends an alien. In the late 1990s, Doordarshan viewers followed *Captain Vyom*, a space hero, every week. The props change with each decade. The questions underneath, about who we are and what we should build, stay much the same.

text: The most famous story says yes. In 1905, an 11-year-old named Frank Epperson, living in the San Francisco Bay Area, mixed soda powder and water in a cup with a wooden stirring stick. He left it outside on the porch overnight. It was an unusually cold night, and by morning the drink had frozen solid around the stick.

He pulled it out by the stick and licked it. Many years later, in 1924, he patented the idea. Today we call it an ice lolly in Britain and India, a popsicle in America, and sometimes an ice candy or chuski at the school gate.

st.prompt: Why does an ice lolly need a freezer colder than 0°C to set properly?

options.t: Sugar in the drink lowers its freezing point

st.reveal: Pure water freezes at 0°C. Sugar and flavourings get in the way of ice crystals forming, so a sweet drink must be colder before it freezes. Home freezers usually run at about minus 18°C, which is plenty.

src: Smithsonian Magazine and NPR (2015), How an 11-year-old boy invented the Popsicle.
U.S. Patent Office, Frank W. Epperson's patent for frozen confectionery (1924).
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ice cream and frozen desserts.
n.certNote: The story of the cold night in 1905 comes from Frank Epperson himself, told many years later, so it can't be checked. His 1924 patent and the Popsicle business are well documented. Frozen sweet treats on sticks or in moulds, such as kulfi, are much older.

myth: Before 1905, nobody had ever eaten a frozen treat on a stick or from a mould.

People were enjoying frozen sweets long before. In India, kulfi was set in metal cones and sold on sticks for generations. Epperson's version made frozen fruit drinks on sticks popular in America and turned them into a business.
facts: kulfi, a frozen milk sweet from the Mughal era

sec.t:
Frank told this story himself, when he was an adult. Nobody wrote it down at the time, so we can't check it. San Francisco rarely gets cold enough to freeze water outdoors, so some people doubt it. Still, frosty nights do happen there now and then, so the tale is possible.

Whether or not every detail is true, the idea stayed with him. For years he made the frozen treats for friends and, later, his own children.

During the [[@great-depression|Great Depression]] of the 1930s, many American families had very little money. Popsicle came up with an idea: a lolly with two sticks that could be snapped in half. Two children could share one treat that cost just a few cents.

That twin design lasted for decades. And the flat wooden sticks became famous on their own, as millions of children used them to build model houses, bridges and puppets.

Pure water freezes at 0°C. But when you [[dissolve|dissolve]] sugar in it, the sugar gets in the way of water [[molecule|molecules]] lining up into ice crystals. The sweeter the drink, the colder it must get before it freezes.

That's why a very sugary lolly stays slightly soft, while a watery one turns rock hard. Home freezers run at about minus 18°C, cold enough for both. The science is close to what happens when [[@ice-cream-freezing|ice cream freezes]], where salt and stirring play a part too.

Long before 1905, India had kulfi. It is a dense frozen milk sweet, flavoured with cardamom, saffron and pistachio. It was being made in north India by the time of the Mughal emperors in the 1500s and 1600s, frozen in metal cones packed into pots of ice and salt.

Kulfi sellers still push their carts through Indian streets, slicing kulfi onto leaves or serving it on a stick. There's also gola, crushed ice pressed onto a stick and soaked with bright syrup. These are cousins of the popsicle, not copies of it.

People in ancient Persia and China also made sweet chilled foods using ice stored from winter. So Epperson didn't invent frozen treats. He made one simple version cheap, easy to hold and easy to sell.

Frank Epperson is often listed among famous [[@inventions-kids|child inventors]]. Louis Braille was 15 when he worked out his raised-dot alphabet for blind readers. Children notice odd things, like a drink frozen around a stick, and ask what could come of it.

One warning comes with every lolly, though. Bite it too fast and a sharp pain stabs your forehead, a strange alarm known as [[@body-brain-freeze|brain freeze]].
